item.title: Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act), Public Law 119-27, 139 Stat. 419

findings.finding: Section 2(22): a payment stablecoin is a digital asset used or designed to be used as a means of payment or settlement whose issuer is obligated to redeem it for a fixed amount of monetary value and represents a stable value; securities, deposits and national currencies are excluded.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (22) Payment stablecoin.--The term ``payment stablecoin''-- (A) means a digital asset-- (i) that is, or is designed to be, used as a means of payment or settlement; and (ii) the issuer of which-- (I) is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value, not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed amount of monetary value; and (II) represents that such issuer will maintain, or create the reasonable expectation that it will maintain, a stable value relative to the value of a fixed amount of monetary value; and

findings.finding: Section 2(23): only three kinds of person are permitted payment stablecoin issuers (insured-depository-institution subsidiary, Federal qualified issuer, State qualified issuer).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (23) Permitted payment stablecoin issuer.--The term ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' means a person formed in the United States that is-- (A) a subsidiary of an insured depository institution that has been approved to issue payment stablecoins under section 5; (B) a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer; or (C) a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.

findings.finding: Section 3(a): issuing a payment stablecoin in the United States is unlawful for anyone other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer; Section 3(f) sets $1,000,000 and 5 years for knowing participation.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (a) Limitation on Issuers.--It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States.

findings.finding: Section 3(b)(1): the digital-asset-service-provider offer/sale prohibition begins three years after enactment (July 18, 2028).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (b) Prohibition on Offers or Sales.-- (1) > In general.--Except as provided in subsection (c) and section 18, beginning on the date that is 3 years after the date of enactment of this Act, it shall be unlawful for a digital asset service provider to offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States, unless the payment stablecoin is issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.

findings.finding: Section 3(h)(1): direct person-to-person transfers and own-custody wallet transactions are outside Section 3.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (h) Rules of Construction.-- (1) Exempt transactions.--This section shall not apply to-- (A) the direct transfer of digital assets between 2 individuals acting on their own behalf and for their own lawful purposes, without the involvement of an intermediary; (B) to any transaction involving the receipt of digital assets by an individual between an account owned by the individual in the United States and an account owned by the individual abroad that are offered by the same parent company; or (C) to any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets.

findings.finding: Section 2(7)(B): the definition of digital asset service provider excludes distributed ledger protocols, their developers, immutable and self-custodial software interfaces, validators, and participation in a liquidity pool.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (B) does not include-- (i) a distributed ledger protocol; (ii) developing, operating, or engaging in the business of developing distributed ledger protocols or self-custodial software interfaces; (iii) an immutable and self-custodial software interface; (iv) developing, operating, or engaging in the business of validating transactions or operating a distributed ledger; or (v) participating in a liquidity pool or other similar mechanism for the provisioning of liquidity for peer-to-peer transactions.

findings.finding: Section 2(24): person includes a cooperative organization.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (24) Person.--The term ``person'' means an individual, partnership, company, corporation, association, trust, estate, cooperative organization, or other business entity, incorporated or unincorporated.

findings.finding: Section 4(a)(11): the yield prohibition binds permitted and foreign payment stablecoin issuers and reaches yield paid solely in connection with holding, use or retention of the stablecoin.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (11) Prohibition on interest.--No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin.

findings.finding: Section 17: a payment stablecoin issued by a permitted issuer is not a security or commodity under the Securities Act, Exchange Act, Investment Company Act, Advisers Act, SIPA or the Commodity Exchange Act.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (c) Securities Act of 1933.--Section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act of 1933 (15 U.S.C. 77b(a)(1)) is amended by adding at the end the following: ``The term `security' does not include a payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, as such terms are defined in section 2 of the GENIUS Act.''.

findings.finding: Section 20: effective on the earlier of 18 months after enactment (January 18, 2027) or 120 days after the primary regulators issue any final implementing regulations.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: This Act, and the amendments made by this Act, shall take effect on the earlier of (1) the date that is 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act; or (2) the date that is 120 days after the date on which the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue any final regulations implementing this Act.

item.title: GENIUS Act Regulations on Payment Stablecoin Issuance, Offer, and Sale (NPRM), 91 FR 53368

findings.finding: Treasury proposes 12 CFR part 1523 to implement Section 3; comments due October 19, 2026. This is a proposal, not a final rule.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: SUMMARY: The Department of the Treasury (Treasury) proposes to issue regulations to implement section 3 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act regarding the statutory prohibitions and limitations on payment stablecoin issuance, offer, and sale in the United States.

findings.finding: Treasury proposes that a payment stablecoin is "issued" when the issuer, directly or through an agent, first transfers it so that a person other than the issuer gets the right to use, transfer or redeem it; crediting an account counts.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Fourth, the first transfer of the payment stablecoin by the issuer must result or will result in a person other than the issuer having the right to use or transfer the payment stablecoin or to have the payment stablecoin converted, redeemed, or repurchased. This element reflects the key features that make a digital asset a payment stablecoin as defined in the Act: its usability as a means of payment or settlement and its convertibility into a fixed amount of monetary value.

findings.finding: Treasury proposes to define "issuer" by the redemption obligation and the stable-value representation, not by minting.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Although the Act defines terms such as ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' and ``foreign payment stablecoin issuer,'' the term ``issuer'' itself is not defined in the Act.

findings.finding: Treasury proposes that a person that issues payment stablecoins for compensation or profit in the United States is also a digital asset service provider.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: with the additional clarification that the term includes a person that, for compensation or profit, engages in the business in the United States of issuing payment stablecoins.

findings.finding: Proposed 1523.4(c) restates the Section 3(h)(1) exempt transactions nearly verbatim, including own-custody wallet transactions.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Proposed Sec. 1523.4(c) implements this provision nearly verbatim and provides that the prohibitions in proposed Sec. 1523.2 and proposed Sec. 1523.3 shall not apply to (i) the direct transfer of digital assets between two individuals acting on their own behalf and for their own lawful purposes, without the involvement of an intermediary; (ii) any transaction involving the receipt of digital assets by an individual between an account owned by the individual in the United States and an account owned by the individual abroad that are offered by the same parent company; and (iii) any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets.

findings.finding: The NPRM heading dates the offer-and-sale prohibition from July 18, 2028.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Offer and Sale Activities On and After July 18, 2028

notFound: No proposed text addresses non-custodial pooling, liquidity pools or yield; the terms "liquidity pool" appear only in questions about bridges and wrapped tokens.

item.title: Implementing the GENIUS Act for the Issuance of Stablecoins by Entities Subject to the Jurisdiction of the OCC (NPRM), 91 FR 10202

findings.finding: Proposed 12 CFR 15.10(c)(4) presumes an issuer pays prohibited yield when it has an arrangement with an affiliate or related third party who in turn pays yield to holders of that issuer's stablecoin; the issuer may rebut in writing.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (4) Pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. (i) The OCC presumes that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is paying interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) to the holder of a payment stablecoin solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin if: (A) The permitted payment stablecoin issuer has a contract, agreement, or other arrangement with an affiliate of the issuer or related third party to pay interest or yield to the affiliate or related third party; (B) The affiliate or related third party identified in paragraph (c)(4)(i)(A) of this section or, if the person is a related third party, an affiliate of such related third party has a contract, agreement, or other arrangement to pay interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) to a holder of any payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin; and (C) To the extent the person, or an affiliate of the person, identified in paragraph (c)(4)(i)(A) is a related third party of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer issues payment stablecoins on the related third party's behalf or under the related third party's branding, the arrangement identified in paragraph (c)(4)(i)(B) of this section considers the holder of the payment stablecoin to be the holder of a payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on the related third party's behalf or under the related third party's branding. (ii) For purposes of paragraph (c)(4)(i) of this section, a related third party means: (A) A person offering to pay interest or yield to payment stablecoin holders as a service; and (B) Any person that the issuer issues payment stablecoins on the person's behalf or under the person's branding. (iii) A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may rebut the presumption in paragraph (c)(4)(i) of this section by submitting written materials that, in the OCC's judgment, demonstrate that the contract, agreement, or other arrangement is not prohibited under paragraph (c)(4) of this section and is not an attempt to evade the prohibition.

findings.finding: A "related third party" is a person offering to pay yield to holders as a service or a person on whose behalf or under whose brand the issuer issues stablecoins.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (ii) For purposes of paragraph (c)(4)(i) of this section, a related third party means: (A) A person offering to pay interest or yield to payment stablecoin holders as a service; and (B) Any person that the issuer issues payment stablecoins on the person's behalf or under the person's branding.

findings.finding: OCC asks whether the prohibition should be broader and what types of rewards should be subject to it (Questions 37 and 38).
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Question 38: Should the prohibition on interest and yield in proposed Sec. 15.10(c)(4) clarify the terms ``pay,'' ``interest,'' ``yield,'' ``solely,'' or any other terms? If so, what clarifications would be helpful? What types of rewards, if any, should be subject to the prohibition?

item.title: H.R. 3633, Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025, as reported to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (Calendar No. 423), 2026-06-01

findings.finding: Section 404(c)(1) of the Senate text would bar a covered party (any digital asset service provider and its affiliates, excluding issuers) from paying interest or yield to a U.S. customer solely for holding payment stablecoins or in a manner economically or functionally equivalent to a deposit.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (c) Prohibition on Interest and Yield.-- (1) In general.--No covered party shall, directly or indirectly, pay any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) to a restricted recipient-- (A) solely in connection with the holding of the payment stablecoins of that restricted recipient; or (B) on a payment stablecoin balance in a manner that is economically or functionally equivalent to the payment of interest or yield on an interest-bearing bank deposit.

findings.finding: Section 404(c)(2)-(3) would permit activity-based and transaction-based rewards, including liquidity provision, collateral posting, governance, validation and staking, and allows them to be calculated by reference to balance, duration or tenure.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (ii) Providing liquidity for market-marking activity, posting of collateral in connection with trading, or otherwise putting assets at credit or investment risk. (iii) The use of any product or service, including participation in governance, validation, staking, or a loyalty, promotional, subscription, or incentive program.

findings.finding: Section 404(a)(4) defines the covered party as a digital asset service provider together with its affiliates, so the Section 2(7)(B) carve-outs of the GENIUS Act decide who is covered.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (4) Covered party.--The term ``covered party'' means any digital asset service provider, together with all of its affiliates, but in each case excluding any permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer registered with the Comptroller.

findings.finding: Section 604 (Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act) would bar treating a non-controlling developer or provider as a money transmitting business under 31 U.S.C. 5330 or 18 U.S.C. 1960.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (c) Treatment.--Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a non- controlling developer or provider-- (1) shall not be treated as-- (A) a money transmitting business, as defined in section 5330 of title 31, United States Code, and the regulations promulgated under that section; or (B) engaged in money transmitting, as defined in section 1960 of title 18, United States Code; and

findings.finding: Section 604(b)(3) defines non-controlling: no legal right or unilateral and independent ability to control, initiate on demand, or effectuate transactions in users' digital assets without a third party's approval.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (3) Non-controlling developer or provider.--The term ``non- controlling developer or provider'' means a developer or provider of a distributed ledger service that, in the regular course of operations, does not have the legal right or the unilateral and independent ability to control, initiate upon demand, or effectuate transactions involving digital assets to which users are entitled, without the approval, consent, or direction of any third party.

findings.finding: Section 604(d) preserves 1960(b)(1)(C) for a person acting with specific intent to transfer funds known to be criminally derived or meant to support unlawful activity.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (d) Clarification of Treatment.--Subsection (c) shall not modify the application of section 1960(b)(1)(C) of title 18, United States Code, to any person (referred to in this subsection as the ``initial person'') that acts with the specific intent to transfer, on behalf of another person, funds that are known by the initial person to be-- (1) derived from a criminal offense; or (2) intended to be used to promote or support unlawful activity.

findings.finding: Section 309 would add Exchange Act Section 15H: no one is subject to the Exchange Act for developing or distributing a decentralized finance trading protocol or wallets, or for participating in a liquidity pool for spot digital commodity purchase or sale.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: ``(5) Developing, publishing, constituting, administering, maintaining, or otherwise distributing a decentralized finance messaging system, or operating or participating in a liquidity pool, for the purpose of executing a spot contract for the purchase or sale of a digital commodity in relation to a decentralized finance trading protocol.

findings.finding: Section 301 defines a decentralized finance trading protocol as an automated, non-discretionary rule system without reliance on a person other than the user for custody; it is excluded when a person or group can materially alter it or censor use.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: (1) Decentralized finance trading protocol.--The term ``decentralized finance trading protocol'' means a distributed ledger system through which multiple participants can execute a financial transaction-- (A) in accordance with an automated rule or algorithm that is predetermined and non-discretionary; and (B) without reliance on a person other than the user to maintain custody or control of any digital assets subject to the financial transaction.

item.title: Application of the Federal Securities Laws to Certain Types of Crypto Assets and Certain Transactions Involving Crypto Assets, 91 FR 13714 (Releases 33-11412; 34-105020)

findings.finding: The Commission restates that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may not pay interest or yield solely for holding the stablecoin, and that stablecoins other than permitted payment stablecoins may be securities depending on facts and circumstances.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: A permitted payment stablecoin issuer is prohibited under the GENIUS Act from paying any form of interest or yield to the permitted stablecoin holders (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of the payment stablecoin.\78\ These crypto assets categorically will not be securities by operation of statute after the effective date of the GENIUS Act. Stablecoins other than payment stablecoins issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may meet the definition of ``security'' depending on the facts and circumstances.

findings.finding: The Commission interprets that offers and sales of "Covered Stablecoins" (those in the April 4, 2025 Staff Stablecoin Statement) are not securities offers; stablecoins other than Covered Stablecoins are not addressed.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: the Commission interprets that, for the reasons set forth in the Staff Stablecoin Statement, the offer and sale of Covered Stablecoins does not involve the offer and sale of securities within the meaning of section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act or section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act.\81\ Accordingly, persons involved in the process of issuing and redeeming Covered Stablecoins do not need to register those transactions with the Commission under the Securities Act or fall within one of the Securities Act's exemptions from registration. The foregoing interpretation does not address stablecoins other than Covered Stablecoins as described in the Staff Stablecoin Statement.

findings.finding: The release states that staff statements have no legal force and that the release supersedes prior staff statements on these topics.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Staff statements have no legal force or effect: they do not alter or amend applicable law, and they create no new or additional obligations for any person. For the avoidance of doubt, the views expressed by the Commission in this release supersede any prior statements by the Commission or its staff on these topics.

notFound: The word "lending" and the term "innovation exemption" do not appear in the release; yield-bearing stablecoin or vault tokens are not addressed.
